title: Gravity, Orbits & Tides
intro: Gravity is the force that holds the Solar System together. Learn how its strength changes with mass and distance (the inverse square law), how it lets us weigh the Sun and planets, how orbits can change or end in escape, and how it raises the tides.

sections.title: Every mass pulls on every other mass

img.alt: Two spheres labelled M1 and M2 pulling on each other across a distance d, with the gravity formula F = G M1 M2 / d squared in a red box below them.

steps.title: The universal law of gravitation
bullets: Every mass attracts every other mass. The Moon, a ball and you all pull on each other.
The pull is **directly proportional** to the **product** of the two masses: bigger masses multiplied together give a bigger force.
The pull is **inversely proportional** to the **square** of the distance between the centers: farther apart gives a much weaker force.

steps.title: The formula
bullets: **F = G M₁ M₂ / d²**. F is the force of gravity, M₁ and M₂ are the two masses, and d is the distance between their centers.
**G** is the **gravitational constant**, a fixed number (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²)). It is very small, so gravity only becomes easy to notice when at least one object is huge.

boxes.text: Why do we measure distance between centers? Gravity acts as if each object's mass sits at its center. When you stand on Earth, you are about one Earth radius (about 6,400 km) from Earth's center, not zero.

Earth pulls on you exactly as hard as you pull on Earth. The two forces are equal and opposite. You are thrown toward Earth and Earth barely moves only because Earth has a gigantic mass, so the same force gives it a tiny acceleration.
Masses go on TOP (more mass, more pull). Distance goes on the BOTTOM and is squared (more distance, much less pull).

Do not mix up the two kinds of change. Double ONE mass: force doubles. Double the DISTANCE: force becomes one quarter, not one half. Practice test 2 Q13 uses factor 4 as the trap answer for a halved mass.

sourceNotes: Gravity deck (Ch4.4_Gravity.pdf) slide 2

sections.title: Inverse square: how the force changes

steps.title: Changing the distance
bullets: Distance doubled: force is **1/4** (2² = 4). Distance tripled: force is **1/9** (3² = 9).
Distance cut in half: force is **4 times** bigger. Distance 10 times bigger: force is 1/100.

steps.title: Changing the masses
bullets: Force is directly proportional to each mass. Double one mass and the force doubles. Halve one mass and the force halves.
Double BOTH masses and the force is 2 × 2 = **4 times** bigger.

steps.title: Mixing changes together
bullets: Turn every change into a factor, then multiply. One mass 3 times bigger and distance 2 times bigger: 3 ÷ (2²) = **3/4**.

steps.title: Worked example: measure from the center
bullets: A satellite feels a pull of 900 N from Earth when it sits on the ground, a distance R from Earth's center.
Lift it to 2R **above the surface**. Its distance from the center is now R + 2R = **3R**, so the force is 900 ÷ 3² = 900 ÷ 9 = **100 N**.
Always measure d from the center of the planet, not from the ground.

boxes.text: Why is the force so sensitive to distance? Because d is squared. A small change in distance changes d² by a bigger factor, so moving twice as far costs you four times the pull.
Method: write each change as a factor. Mass changes go on top as they are. Distance changes go on the bottom squared. Multiply and simplify.
Halving a mass gives a factor of 2 (not 4). Doubling the distance gives a factor of 4 (not 2). The practice questions test exactly this swap (practice test 2 Q13, extra practice Q17).

sections.title: Orbits can be ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas
sections.slides: Gravity deck: 3; Cosmic Perspective Figures 4.18 and 4.19 (pp. 124-125)

img.alt: A bound elliptical orbit around an orange dot, with two open curved paths, an unbound parabolic orbit and an unbound hyperbolic orbit, leaving it.

steps.title: Bound and unbound orbits
bullets: Kepler's laws work for **every** orbiting object (moons, satellites, asteroids), not just planets.
A **bound** orbit is an **ellipse**. The object goes around again and again.
An **unbound** orbit is a parabola or a **hyperbola**. The object swings past once and never comes back.

img.alt: Left: a bound elliptical orbit with an unbound parabolic and an unbound hyperbolic orbit. Right: a cone sliced at different angles to make a circle, an ellipse, a parabola and a hyperbola.

steps.title: Orbit shapes are conic sections
bullets: Circles and ellipses are bound. Parabolas and hyperbolas are unbound. All four shapes come from slicing a cone at different angles.
Far from the center a hyperbolic orbit looks almost like a straight line.
Objects on unbound orbits still move faster when they are closer to the object they pass.

steps.title: Newton explained Kepler's laws
bullets: The inverse square law of gravity leads naturally to elliptical orbits with the Sun at one **focus**.
Kepler's second law (faster when closer) follows from conservation of angular momentum, and the third law follows from gravity weakening with distance.

img.alt: Three pairs of objects joined by a line with a black triangle at the balance point: equal stars with the point halfway, a heavy and a light star with the point nearer the heavy one, and a star and a tiny planet with the point inside the star.

steps.title: Orbiting a common center of mass
bullets: Two objects pulled together by gravity both orbit their **center of mass**, the point where they would balance.
Equal masses: the point is halfway between them. Unequal masses: it lies closer to the heavier object.
A star and a planet: the point is inside or almost inside the star, so we barely notice the star's wobble.

boxes.text: Why is it called bound? Gravity creates a bond that holds the two objects together, so a bound object keeps returning. An unbound object has too much energy for the bond to hold.
Ellipse comes back. Parabola and hyperbola say bye.

In an ellipse the Sun is at one FOCUS, not at the center of the ellipse. A practice question (test 1 Q23) lists 'the Sun at the center of the ellipse' as the statement that does NOT follow from Kepler's first law. Also comets and asteroids need not follow ellipses: some comets are on unbound orbits.

sections.title: Weighing worlds with Newton's version of Kepler's third law
sections.slides: Gravity deck: 4-5; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.3 and Figure 4.20 (pp. 125-126)

img.alt: The formula p squared equals 4 pi squared over G times (M1 + M2), times a cubed, in a red box.

steps.title: The formula and what it tells us
bullets: **p² = 4π² a³ / [G (M₁ + M₂)]**. p is the orbital period, a is the average orbital distance, and M₁ + M₂ is the total mass of the two objects.
Measure the period and the distance of an orbit and the formula gives the **total mass**.
Earth's period (1 year) and distance (1 AU) give the Sun's mass. A satellite's orbit gives Earth's mass. A moon of Jupiter gives Jupiter's mass.

steps.title: Using it in simple cases
bullets: For orbits around the Sun, with p in years and a in AU, the formula becomes Kepler's simple **p² = a³**. An object at 4 AU has p² = 64, so p = 8 years.
Keep the same orbit size but make the total mass 4 times bigger: p² becomes 1/4, so the period is **cut in half**.
A small object orbiting a huge one (Phobos and Mars): M₁ + M₂ is almost just the big mass, so the formula gives the big object's mass.

steps.title: Worked example: the Sun's mass
bullets: Earth: p = 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s and a = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Earth is tiny, so M(Sun) + M(Earth) is about M(Sun).
Solve for the mass: **M(Sun) = 4π² a³ / (G p²)** = 4π² (1.5 × 10¹¹)³ / [6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (3.15 × 10⁷)²].
The result is about **2 × 10³⁰ kg**.

steps.title: Worked example: a geosynchronous satellite
bullets: A geosynchronous satellite orbits once per sidereal day (86,164 s), so it stays above the same spot on Earth.
Solving the same formula for the distance gives a ≈ **42,000 km** from Earth's center.
Earth's radius is about 6,400 km, so the satellite is about 35,600 km above the surface.

img.alt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit floating beside a spacecraft with Earth below.

steps.title: Why an astronaut needs no tether
bullets: For a small object circling a much heavier one, the period depends only on the orbital distance, not on the small object's mass.
The astronaut and the spacecraft are both tiny compared with Earth and share the same orbit, so they have the same period and stay together at about 28,000 km/hr.

boxes.text: Why do an orbit's period and size reveal mass? A more massive center pulls harder, so at the same distance the orbiter moves faster and finishes a lap sooner. Reading the period and distance backwards tells you how strong the pull, and so how big the mass, must be.
Period and distance IN, total mass OUT.

Practice test 2 Q14 (Mars and Phobos): the official answer is A, 'orbital period and speed', because distance around the orbit = speed x period gives the orbit size (the explained file says so). Distance alone (option D) and the small moon's own mass (option E) are wrong. You always need the period together with the orbit size.

sections.title: Orbital energy stays constant
sections.slides: Orbits and Tides deck: 2; Cosmic Perspective Figure 4.21 (p. 126)

img.alt: A tall ellipse with a yellow Sun near the bottom: at the top the object is slow with more potential energy, at the bottom it is fast with more kinetic energy.

steps.title: Kinetic plus potential equals constant
bullets: **Total orbital energy** = gravitational potential energy + kinetic energy. It stays the same when no outside force acts.
Farther from the Sun: more potential energy, less kinetic energy, so slower.

steps.title: Orbits do not change by themselves
bullets: Because energy is conserved, an orbit cannot change spontaneously.
Left alone, planets and moons would keep the same orbits forever. A change in the total energy is needed to change the shape of an orbit.

boxes.text: Why does a planet speed up when it gets closer? Think of a roller coaster. Falling toward the Sun turns potential energy into kinetic energy, and climbing away turns it back. The sum stays fixed.
Low and fast, high and slow, but the total never changes.

Only the split between potential and kinetic changes along the orbit. The TOTAL stays constant. Practice test 2 Q9: a planet on an ellipse feels a varying gravity force because its distance varies (inverse square law), which is why it speeds up and slows down.

sections.title: How an orbit gains or loses energy
sections.slides: Orbits and Tides deck: 3; Cosmic Perspective Figure 4.22 (p. 127)

img.alt: A comet's dashed unbound path bending as it passes Jupiter and becoming a closed elliptical orbit around the yellow Sun.

steps.title: A gravitational encounter
bullets: A comet on an unbound orbit passes close to Jupiter. The two swap orbital energy.
The comet loses so much energy that its orbit changes from unbound to a bound ellipse.
Jupiter gains exactly what the comet loses, but its huge mass hides the effect.

steps.title: Three ways to change orbital energy
bullets: **Friction or atmospheric drag**. Not important in empty space, but it matters in a thin atmosphere.
A **gravitational encounter**: a close pass by another object swaps energy between the two.
**Collisions or impacts**.

steps.title: Examples
bullets: A satellite in low Earth orbit meets a little drag from the thin upper air. It loses orbital energy as heat, slowly falls and often burns up.
The New Horizons spacecraft was sent past Jupiter on purpose to gain orbital energy at Jupiter's expense. This saved about four years on the trip to Pluto.
Encounters with the giant planets probably kicked many comets out into far-away orbits.

boxes.text: Why do orbits only change when something acts on the object? The orbit's energy is fixed unless energy is passed to or taken from another object. Energy is moved around, never created.
Drag, Encounter, Collision: the three ways to change an orbit's energy.

The slide says drag is 'not usually applicable in space', but the textbook and the practice questions (extra practice Q19) show a low Earth orbit satellite DOES lose energy to the thin upper atmosphere. The orbital energy DECREASES, not increases.

sections.title: Escape velocity
sections.slides: Orbits and Tides deck: 4; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.4 and Figure 4.23 (pp. 127-128)

img.alt: Earth with a low circular orbit, a bigger elliptical orbit and a path that leaves Earth, labelled escape velocity, with notes on firing a rocket a little or for long enough.

steps.title: Leaving for good
bullets: Firing a rocket a little gives extra orbital energy and lifts the spacecraft into a higher, more elliptical orbit.
Firing long enough gives enough energy to change a bound orbit into an unbound one, and the spacecraft escapes.
**Escape velocity** from Earth is about **11 km/s** from sea level, roughly 40,000 km/hr.

steps.title: What it does and does not depend on
bullets: It does **not** depend on the mass of the escaping object. An atom, a rock and a spacecraft all need about 11 km/s.
It does depend on the planet and on the starting distance: **v = √(2GM/R)**. Starting higher up needs less speed, because gravity is weaker there.

steps.title: Worked example: the Moon
bullets: Moon: M = 7.4 × 10²² kg and R = 1.7 × 10⁶ m (its radius, since we start on the surface).
That is less than one-fourth of Earth's 11 km/s.

steps.title: Worked example: from a high station
bullets: A station in geosynchronous orbit is 42,000 km (4.2 × 10⁷ m) from Earth's center. Earth's mass is 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg.
That is far less than 11 km/s, so launching from a high station needs much less fuel.

boxes.text: Why does the object's own mass not matter? A heavier object needs more energy to climb out, but it also carries more energy at the same speed. The two scale together, so the needed speed is the same.
Eleven km/s is about 40,000 km/hr: the same speed in two units. Remember the small number, 11, for the exam.

Eleven km/s is not the speed of light (about 300,000 km/s). It is also not the same for every planet and not bigger when you start farther away (practice Q20 options B, C, D). Slide and textbook agree on 11 km/s and 40,000 km/hr.

sections.title: How gravity causes tides
sections.slides: Orbits and Tides deck: 5; Cosmic Perspective Figures 4.24 and 4.26 (pp. 128-130)

img.alt: Earth inside an oval of blue ocean with three arrows pointing toward a small grey Moon, the arrow on the near side the longest.

steps.title: The Moon stretches Earth
bullets: The Moon's gravity is stronger on the near side of Earth than on the far side.
This difference slightly **stretches** Earth along the Earth-Moon line.

img.alt: Earth inside an oval of blue ocean with arrows toward the Moon and notes that the pull is weakest on the far side and strongest on the near side, raising bulges both toward and away from the Moon.

steps.title: Two bulges, two high tides
bullets: Stretching makes two **tidal bulges**: one toward the Moon and one on the opposite side.
Earth spins through both bulges each day, so most places get two high tides and two low tides. The cycle takes about 24 h 50 min, so high tides come about 12 h 25 min apart.
The bulges raise the oceans only about 2 meters and the land only about a centimeter.

img.alt: Two diagrams: at new Moon and full Moon the Sun and Moon pull along the same line and make spring tides, at first- and third-quarter Moon they pull at right angles and make smaller neap tides.

steps.title: Spring and neap tides
bullets: The Sun also makes tides, a little less than half as strong as the Moon's.
At **new Moon and full Moon** the Sun and Moon pull along the same line and the tides are largest: **spring tides**.
At first and third quarter Moon they work against each other and the tides are smaller: **neap tides**.

steps.title: Why the Sun's tides are weaker
bullets: The Sun's pull on Earth as a whole is much stronger than the Moon's. That is why Earth orbits the Sun.
Tides come from the **difference** in pull between the near and far sides, and at the Sun's huge distance that difference is small.

boxes.text: Why is there a bulge on the side AWAY from the Moon? Think of a rubber band: pull one side and it stretches in both directions from its center. Earth's near side is pulled hardest, its center less, its far side least, so Earth is stretched along the Earth-Moon line.
Why is the Sun's tide weaker even though the Sun is far more massive? Tides come from the DIFFERENCE in pull across Earth, and at the Sun's huge distance that difference is small.
Spring is when the water springs up: new and full Moon, with Sun, Earth and Moon in a line.

Tides are not simply the Moon pulling the water toward it (that would give one bulge, not two). Spring tides have nothing to do with the season. The slides do not mention spring or neap tides, so those come from the textbook; practice Q21 has no answer key but the textbook gives new and full Moon.

sections.title: Tidal friction and the Moon's locked face
sections.slides: Orbits and Tides deck: 6; Cosmic Perspective Figure 4.27 (p. 130)

img.alt: Earth with a tidal bulge tilted slightly ahead of the dashed Earth-Moon line, with arrows showing Earth's spin, the Moon's pull back on the bulge, and the bulge's pull forward on the Moon.

steps.title: The bulge leads the Moon
bullets: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so the tidal bulge is dragged slightly **ahead** of the Earth-Moon line. It acts like a handle for the Moon's gravity.
The Moon pulls back on the bulge, so **Earth's rotation slows**. The bulge pulls the Moon forward, so the Moon gains orbital energy and moves **farther away**.

steps.title: Synchronous rotation and the numbers
bullets: The Moon once spun much faster. Tidal friction slowed its spin until it locked into **synchronous rotation**: it turns once per orbit and always shows nearly the same face to Earth.
Tidal friction lengthens Earth's day by only about 1 second every 50,000 years, but over billions of years it adds up.
Long ago a day may have been only 5 or 6 hours long, and the Moon may have been one-tenth of its present distance or less.

boxes.text: Why is this a good example of conservation? The angular momentum and energy that Earth loses as it slows are gained by the Moon as it moves outward.
Earth spins, the bulge runs ahead, and the bulge tugs the Moon forward. Earth slows down, the Moon moves out.

Practice test 2 Q16 traps: the Moon's synchronous rotation is about its SPIN, not its distance; Earth's rotation is slowing, not speeding up; eclipses add no energy; and the pairs of tidal forces do not give a steady push outward. The correct reason is that Earth's tidal bulge pulls the Moon forward.

sections.title: Why every object falls at the same rate

img.alt: Two portraits side by side, Isaac Newton on the left and Albert Einstein on the right.

steps.title: Force differs, acceleration does not
bullets: The **force** of gravity depends on the masses. The **acceleration** of a falling object does not depend on its own mass.
A heavier rock feels a bigger pull, but it also has more inertia (it resists acceleration more). The two cancel exactly.
Newton found this strange. It was not understood until Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915).

steps.title: The acceleration of gravity
bullets: Near Earth's surface the acceleration of gravity is about **9.8 m/s²** for every falling object.
From F = G M₁ M₂ / d² the acceleration of a rock is a = G M(Earth) / d². The rock's mass cancels, and a drops to 1/4 if d doubles.

steps.title: Worked examples: Moon and Space Station
bullets: Moon: g = GM/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.4 × 10²² ÷ (1.7 × 10⁶)² ≈ **1.7 m/s²**, about one-sixth of Earth's, so things weigh about one-sixth as much.
That is only about 10% less than at the surface. Astronauts float because they are in free-fall, not because gravity is missing.

boxes.text: Why does the mass cancel? Gravity's force on the rock is proportional to the rock's mass, and then F = ma divides by the rock's mass to get the acceleration. Whatever mass you start with disappears.
Big rock, big pull, but also big laziness. They cancel.

Do not confuse force and acceleration. The force of gravity is NOT the same for all objects (practice test 2 Q15 option C is the trap). Only the acceleration is the same. Parabolas and hyperbolas are explained by Newton, so they are not the unexplained feature.

cards.back: It loses orbital energy (turned into heat) and gradually falls toward Earth.
A comet passing Jupiter can lose orbital energy to Jupiter and change from an unbound to a bound orbit.
About 11 km/s from sea level, roughly 40,000 km/hr.

cards.front: Does escape velocity depend on the object's mass?
cards.back: No. Atoms, rocks and spacecraft all need about 11 km/s to leave Earth.
cards.short: Not dependent on the object's mass

cards.back: The Moon's gravity is stronger on Earth's near side than on its far side, and the difference stretches Earth.
Two: one toward the Moon and one away. Earth rotates through both, giving two high tides a day.
cards.short: Two tidal bulges, two daily highs

cards.back: The largest tides, at new Moon and full Moon when the Sun and Moon pull along the same line.
cards.short: Largest tides: new and full Moon

cards.back: The smallest tides, at first and third quarter Moon when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
It slows Earth's rotation and pulls the Moon ahead in its orbit, so the Moon moves farther away.
cards.src: Orbits and Tides deck slide 6; practice test 2 Q16

cards.back: The Moon turns once per orbit, so it always shows nearly the same face to Earth. Tidal friction slowed its once-faster spin.
It does not depend on the object's own mass. Einstein's general relativity (1915) explained why.
cards.short: All objects fall at same rate
cards.src: Orbits and Tides deck slide 7; practice test 2 Q15

cards.front: Acceleration of gravity at Earth's surface
cards.back: About 9.8 m/s².
About 12 h 25 min, because the full cycle of two highs takes about 24 h 50 min.
cards.short: High tides about 12 h 25 min apart

cards.back: v = √(2GM/R), where M is the mass of the planet or moon and R is the starting distance from its center. It gives 2.4 km/s from the Moon's surface and 4.4 km/s from geosynchronous orbit.
g = GM/R². It is 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface, 1.7 m/s² on the Moon and 8.8 m/s² at the Space Station's altitude.

cards.front: Common center of mass in an orbit
cards.back: Two objects held by gravity both orbit the point where they would balance. It is halfway for equal masses and closer to the heavier object. For the Sun and a planet it is inside or almost inside the Sun.

quiz.q: According to the universal law of gravitation, if the distance between two objects is tripled, the gravitational force between them will
quiz.why: Force goes as 1/d². Tripling d makes d² nine times bigger, so the force is one ninth as strong.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q17; Gravity deck slide 2

quiz.q: According to the universal law of gravitation, if the mass of one of the attracting bodies is halved, the gravitational force between them will
quiz.why: Force is directly proportional to each mass, so half the mass gives half the force. The factor 4 is what you get from changing the distance, not a mass.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q13 and its explained file; Gravity deck slide 2

quiz.q: Two objects attract each other with a force F. The mass of the first object is tripled, the mass of the second object is halved, and the distance between their centers is tripled. The new force is
quiz.why: Write each change as a factor: the masses give 3 × 1/2 = 3/2 on top, and tripling d divides by 3² = 9. So the force is (3/2) ÷ 9 = 1/6 of F. F/2 forgets to square the distance factor.
quiz.source: Gravity deck slide 2 (F = G M1 M2 / d^2); Cosmic Perspective 4.4; calculation

quiz.q: A satellite feels a gravitational force of 900 N from Earth while it sits on the ground, a distance R from Earth's center. It is then lifted to an altitude of 2R above Earth's surface. What is the force of Earth's gravity on it now?
quiz.why: Distance is measured from the center. At 2R above the surface, d = R + 2R = 3R, so the force is 900 ÷ 3² = 900 ÷ 9 = 100 N. Using d = 2R gives the wrong 225 N, and 8,100 N multiplies by 9 instead of dividing.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.4 (Figure 4.17: d is between centers); calculation

quiz.q: In which of the following situations is Newton's third law NOT applicable?
options: when one object is much more massive than the other
Newton's third law is applicable in all cases.
when the force in question is gravity and the objects are physically separated
when more than two objects are involved
quiz.why: Every force comes as an equal and opposite pair. Earth pulls on you exactly as hard as you pull on Earth. The different masses only give different accelerations, not different forces. The law also holds for gravity at a distance.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q10 and its explained file

quiz.q: Which of the following statements does NOT follow from Kepler's first law?
options: Comets and asteroids need not orbit the Sun in elliptical paths.
The Sun is located at one of the ellipse foci, while the other focus need not be occupied by any other body.
Venus, Mars, and the other planets orbit the Sun.
The orbits of planets are elliptical with the Sun at the center of the ellipse.
quiz.why: In an ellipse the Sun sits at one focus, not at the center. All the other statements are consistent with Kepler's first law and with Newton's extension of it.
quiz.source: Practice test 1 Q23 and its explained file; Cosmic Perspective 4.4

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about orbits under gravity.
I. An object on a hyperbolic orbit still moves faster when it is closer to the object it passes.
II. A comet on an unbound orbit swings around the Sun once and never returns.
III. A planet orbits a Sun that stays perfectly still at the center of the system.
quiz.why: I and II are true: even unbound orbits obey the rule that an object moves faster when closer. III is false: the Sun and the planet both orbit their common center of mass, which lies inside or almost inside the Sun.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.4 (pp. 124-125, Figures 4.18-4.19)

quiz.q: Two stars with masses 2M and M are 9 AU apart (the middle diagram in the picture). They both orbit their common center of mass. How far is the center of mass from the more massive star?
quiz.why: The balance point lies closer to the heavier star, so the distances are in the ratio 1 : 2 (the heavier star is half as far as the lighter one). The two distances add to 9 AU, so 3 AU and 6 AU. 4.5 AU would be correct only for equal masses.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.4 and Figure 4.19 (p. 125); (outside source) the 1:2 balance arithmetic follows from the textbook definition of the center of mass as the point where the objects would balance

img.alt: Three pairs of objects joined by a line with a black triangle at the balance point: equal stars, a heavy and a light star, and a star and a tiny planet.

quiz.q: Earth orbits the Sun in 1 year (3.15 × 10⁷ s) at an average distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Use Newton's version of Kepler's third law, p² = 4π² a³ / [G (M₁ + M₂)], with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²). Because Earth is tiny, M₁ + M₂ is about the Sun's mass. The Sun's mass is about
quiz.why: Solve for M = 4π² a³ / (G p²). The top is 39.5 × (1.5 × 10¹¹)³ = 1.33 × 10³⁵. The bottom is 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (3.15 × 10⁷)² = 6.62 × 10⁴. Dividing gives 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg. Forgetting to square p gives 6 × 10³⁷, forgetting 4π² gives 5 × 10²⁸, and putting a in km gives 2 × 10²¹.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.3, Example 1 (p. 126); Gravity deck slide 5

quiz.q: A geosynchronous satellite is 42,000 km from Earth's center and has an orbital period of 24 hours. The Space Station orbits Earth at 6,750 km from Earth's center. Both are tiny compared with Earth. About how long does the Space Station take to orbit once?
quiz.why: Same central mass, so p² is proportional to a³. The distance ratio is 6,750 ÷ 42,000 = 0.161, so p = 24 h × 0.161^1.5 = 24 × 0.0644 = 1.55 h. Using p proportional to a gives 3.9 h, p to a² gives 0.6 h, p to a³ gives 0.1 h and p to √a gives 9.6 h.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.3 Example 2 (42,000 km) and Mathematical Insight 4.5 Example 2 (6,750 km); Newton's version of Kepler's third law; calculation

quiz.q: A planet orbits at 1 AU, the same distance as Earth, around a star whose mass is 4 times the Sun's mass. Using Newton's version of Kepler's third law, its orbital period is
quiz.why: p² = 4π² a³ / [G (M₁ + M₂)]. The distance is the same, but the total mass is 4 times bigger, so p² is 4 times smaller. The square root of 1/4 is 1/2, so the period is half a year. A heavier star pulls harder, so the planet finishes a lap sooner.
quiz.source: Gravity deck slides 4-5; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.3; calculation

quiz.q: Which of the following is the best way of determining the mass of Mars by examining its moon Phobos?
options: Phobos's orbital period and speed tell us the mass of Mars, via Newton's version of Kepler's third law.
The gravitational acceleration of Phobos towards Mars tells us the mass of Mars, via Newton's second law.
Phobos's orbital eccentricity tells us Mars's mass, via Newton's version of Kepler's second law.
Phobos's orbital distance alone tells us the mass of Mars, via the universal law of gravitation.
Phobos's mass alone tells us the mass of Mars, via the universal law of gravitation.
quiz.why: Distance around the orbit = speed × period, so period and speed give the orbit size. Period and size in Newton's version of Kepler's third law give the total mass, and since Phobos is tiny that is almost all Mars. Distance alone is not enough, and Phobos's own mass tells us nothing about Mars.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q14 and its explained file (answer A); Gravity deck slides 4-5

quiz.q: Consider Newton's second law, F = ma. If a planet is travelling in an elliptical orbit, what does that imply about the force acting on the planet?
options: The constant acceleration of the planet, as evidenced by its orbital path, arises from the constant gravitational force acting on it.
Newton's second law does not apply to orbits; we require Kepler's laws for explaining orbital mechanics.
The varying acceleration of the planet, as evidenced by its orbital path, arises from a varying gravitational force acting on it.
The mass and the acceleration of the planet vary over the course of the orbit in order to maintain a constant gravitational force.
There is no force acting on the planet; that is why it doesn't slow down or speed up in its orbit.
quiz.why: On an ellipse the distance to the Sun keeps changing. Gravity follows an inverse square law, so a changing distance means a changing force and a changing acceleration. The planet's mass does not change.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q9 and its explained file (answer C)

quiz.q: During a space walk, an astronaut drifting next to the Space Station does not need a tether to stay close to it. The best explanation is that
options: the Space Station's gravity is strong enough to hold the astronaut.
there is no gravity in orbit, so nothing pulls them apart.
heavier objects orbit faster, and the astronaut and the Station have equal masses.
both are tiny compared with Earth and share the same orbital distance, so they have the same orbital period.
the thin air at that height drags both objects along together.
quiz.why: Newton's version of Kepler's third law shows that for a small object circling a much heavier one, the period depends only on the orbital distance, not on the small object's mass. Same distance means same period, so they stay together even at about 28,000 km/hr.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Figure 4.20, p. 125)

img.alt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit floating beside a spacecraft with Earth below.

quiz.q:
In the picture, a planet moves on an elliptical orbit around the Sun. Compare its closest point with its farthest point.
I. Its gravitational potential energy is lower at the closest point.
II. Its kinetic energy is higher at the closest point.
III. Its total orbital energy is lower at the closest point.
quiz.why: Closer to the Sun means less potential energy and faster motion, so more kinetic energy: I and II are true. The two changes cancel in the sum, so the total orbital energy is the same everywhere: III is false.
quiz.source: Orbits and Tides deck slide 2; Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Figure 4.21, p. 126)

img.alt: An elliptical orbit with the Sun inside: closer to the Sun the object has a smaller distance, less potential energy and faster speed; farther away it has more potential energy and slower speed.

quiz.q: The picture shows a comet on an unbound orbit that passes close to Jupiter and ends up on a bound elliptical orbit around the Sun. Which statement is correct?
options: The comet lost orbital energy to Jupiter, and Jupiter gained exactly that much, though the effect on Jupiter's huge mass cannot be noticed.
The comet gained orbital energy from Jupiter, which is why its orbit became smaller.
The comet's orbit changed spontaneously, because orbits are not fixed.
The comet and Jupiter both lost orbital energy, which turned into heat.
The comet's total energy did not change; only its direction was bent.
quiz.why: An orbit can change only through an exchange of energy. The comet lost enough energy to go from unbound to bound, and energy is conserved, so Jupiter gained exactly what the comet lost.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Figure 4.22, p. 127); Orbits and Tides deck slide 3

img.alt: A comet's dashed unbound path bending as it passes Jupiter and becoming a closed elliptical orbit around the yellow Sun.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a way for an object to gain or lose orbital energy?
options: A gravitational encounter with another object
The orbit changing by itself with no outside influence
quiz.why: Orbits cannot change spontaneously. Energy has to be exchanged with something else.
quiz.source: Orbits and Tides deck slides 2-3; Cosmic Perspective 4.5

quiz.q: A satellite in low Earth orbit slowly loses altitude because of drag from the thin upper atmosphere. What happens to its orbital energy?
options: It increases, so the satellite moves to a higher orbit.
It is converted into extra mass for the satellite.
It is transferred to the Moon.
It decreases, turning into heat, so the satellite gradually falls toward Earth.
quiz.why: Drag takes orbital energy away as thermal energy, so the orbit shrinks until the satellite falls and often burns up.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q19; Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Atmospheric Drag, p. 127)

quiz.q: Which statement about escape velocity from Earth is TRUE?
options: It is about 11 km/s from the surface, no matter how massive the object is.
A heavier spacecraft needs a higher escape velocity.
It is the same for every planet in the solar system.
It is larger the farther you start from Earth.
quiz.why: Escape velocity does not depend on the escaping object's mass. 300,000 km/s is the speed of light. It depends on the planet's mass and size, and it is lower if you start higher up.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q20; Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Escape Velocity, pp. 127-128)

quiz.q: The escape velocity from a planet or moon is v = √(2GM/R). Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²), the Moon's mass 7.4 × 10²² kg and the Moon's radius 1.7 × 10⁶ m. The escape velocity from the Moon's surface is about
quiz.why: 2GM = 2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.4 × 10²² = 9.87 × 10¹². Dividing by R = 1.7 × 10⁶ m gives 5.8 × 10⁶, and the square root is about 2,400 m/s = 2.4 km/s. Forgetting the 2 gives 1.7 km/s, and forgetting the square root gives 5.8 × 10⁶ m/s.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.4, Example 1 (p. 128)

quiz.q: Earth's escape velocity from the surface is 11 km/s. Using v = √(2GM/R), what is the escape velocity for a probe that starts 4 Earth radii from Earth's center (R = 4 R_Earth)?
quiz.why: The starting distance is 4 times bigger, and v is proportional to 1/√R. The square root of 4 is 2, so the speed is halved: 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5 km/s. Dividing by 4 would forget the square root. The speed is not the same, because gravity is weaker higher up.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.4 (pp. 127-128), same method as Example 2; calculation

quiz.q: The Space Station orbits 350 km above Earth's surface, which is 6,750 km from Earth's center. Earth's radius is 6,400 km and g at the surface is 9.8 m/s². Which statement is correct?
options: Gravity there is nearly zero, which is why astronauts float.
Gravity there is about 8.8 m/s², only about 10% weaker than at the surface, and astronauts float because they are in free-fall.
Gravity there is about 4.9 m/s², half of the surface value, because the Station is hundreds of kilometers up.
Gravity there is about 9.8 m/s², exactly as at the surface, and astronauts float because of the vacuum.
Gravity there is about 8.8 m/s², and astronauts float because their mass is zero in orbit.
quiz.why: g goes as 1/d². The distance ratio is 6,400 ÷ 6,750 = 0.948, and squared that is 0.899, so g = 9.8 × 0.899 = 8.8 m/s². Gravity is far from zero. Astronauts feel weightless because they and the Station are falling together, and their mass does not change.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 4.5, Example 2 (p. 131); calculation

quiz.q: Which of the following is a strange feature of Newton's gravitational theory that went unexplained until about 110 years ago?
options: Non-elliptical orbit shapes, including parabolas and hyperbolas, can be observed, which are not explained in Newtonian gravity.
The force of gravity is the same for all objects at a given height above Earth's surface, regardless of their physical characteristics or properties.
Gravity drops off rapidly as the distance between objects increases, unlike every other force.
Gravity is the only force that acts at a distance, without the two objects being in physical contact.
The acceleration of gravity is the same for all objects at a given height above Earth's surface, regardless of their physical characteristics or properties.
quiz.why: A heavy rock feels a bigger pull but also has more inertia, and the two cancel exactly, so all objects fall with the same acceleration. Einstein explained why in 1915. The force is not the same (it depends on mass), and Newton did explain parabolas and hyperbolas.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q15 and its explained file (answer B); Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (p. 131)

quiz.q: The picture shows the Moon's pull on three places along a line through Earth. Which statement best explains why Earth has two tidal bulges?
options: The Moon's pull is strongest on the near side and weakest on the far side, and this difference stretches Earth along the Earth-Moon line.
The Moon pushes the far-side water away from itself.
The Sun pulls the far-side water in the opposite direction at the same moment.
The Moon pulls the near-side water toward it and Earth's spin throws the far-side water outward.
The Moon's pull is the same everywhere on Earth, but Earth's rotation makes two bulges.
quiz.why: Tides come from the difference in pull across Earth. Like a rubber band pulled on one side only, Earth stretches in both directions from its center, giving bulges toward and away from the Moon.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Figure 4.24 and the 'Origin of Tides' box, pp. 128-129); Orbits and Tides deck slide 5

img.alt: Earth inside an oval of blue ocean with arrows toward the Moon, the arrow on the near side longest, and notes about bulges toward and away from the Moon.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about the Sun's and the Moon's effects on Earth.
I. The Sun's gravitational pull on Earth is much stronger than the Moon's.
II. The Sun's tidal force on Earth is more than twice the Moon's.
III. The Sun's tidal force is the smaller one because tides come from the difference in pull across Earth, and that difference is small at the Sun's great distance.
quiz.why: I is true: Earth orbits the Sun because of this strong pull. II is false: the Sun's tidal force is a little less than half the Moon's. III is the correct reason.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (The Tidal Effect of the Sun, p. 129)

quiz.q: When do the largest (spring) tides occur?
options: When the Moon is at its farthest from Earth
At new Moon and full Moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up
When Earth is farthest from the Sun
quiz.why: At new and full Moon the tidal forces of the Sun and Moon work together. At the quarter Moons they work against each other and give small neap tides.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Figure 4.26, p. 130); ASTR207 Practice questions Q21 (no answer key; answer from Cosmic Perspective 4.5)

img.alt: Two diagrams of Earth with arrows: at new and full Moon the Sun and Moon pull along the same line, at first and third quarter Moon they pull at right angles.

quiz.q: High tide at a beach occurs at 3:10 pm on Monday. Assume two high tides in each tidal cycle and that the cycle of two highs and two lows takes 24 h 50 min. When is the high tide AFTER the next one?
quiz.why: The next high tide comes 12 h 25 min later, at 3:35 am Tuesday. The one after that comes a full cycle of 24 h 50 min after the first: 3:10 pm Monday + 24 h = 3:10 pm Tuesday, plus 50 min = 4:00 pm Tuesday. A 24 h cycle would be wrong because the Moon takes about 24 h 50 min to return overhead.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (p. 129); calculation

quiz.q: Which of the following explains why the Moon is farther from Earth than it used to be?
options: Earth's tidal bulge pulls the Moon forward in its orbit, giving it orbital energy.
Synchronous rotation locked one face of the Moon toward Earth, so the Moon's orbit grew.
The Moon gains orbital energy every time it lines up with the Sun in an eclipse.
Earth's rotation is speeding up, which pulls the Moon ahead.
The Moon's own tides push it away from Earth every year.
quiz.why: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so its bulge sits ahead of the Moon and tugs it forward. The Moon gains orbital energy and moves outward while Earth's spin slows.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q16 and its explained file; Orbits and Tides deck slide 6

quiz.q: Tidal friction lengthens Earth's day by about 1 second every 50,000 years. If the rate stayed the same, how much longer would the day be after 100 million years?
quiz.why: Divide the time by 50,000 years per second: 100,000,000 ÷ 50,000 = 2,000. So the day gets 2,000 s longer, which is about 33 minutes. Tiny changes add up over huge times.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (Tidal Friction, p. 130); calculation

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about the Moon's synchronous rotation.
I. Earth's tidal force on the Moon is stronger than the Moon's tidal force on Earth, because Earth is more massive.
II. The Moon once spun faster, and tidal friction slowed its spin until it matched its orbital period, which ended the friction.
III. Synchronous rotation means the Moon does not rotate at all.
quiz.why: I and II are true. III is false: the Moon turns once for each orbit, so it does rotate, and that is why we always see nearly the same face.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 4.5 (The Moon's Synchronous Rotation, p. 130); Orbits and Tides deck slide 6

order.title: Strongest to weakest pull
order.prompt: The same two masses are placed at different distances apart. Put the situations in order from the strongest gravitational pull (bottom) to the weakest pull (top).
order.why: Gravity follows F = G M₁ M₂ / d². At half the distance the force is 4 times bigger. At the original distance it is F. At twice the distance it is F/4, at three times the distance F/9, and at ten times the distance F/100.

order.title: Hardest to easiest escape
order.prompt: Put these starting points in order from the one that needs the HIGHEST escape velocity (bottom) to the one that needs the LOWEST (top).
order.why: Escape velocity is v = √(2GM/R). From Earth's surface it is 11 km/s. From 4 Earth radii it is half of that, 5.5 km/s. From a geosynchronous station at 42,000 km it is 4.4 km/s. From the Moon's surface, with its small mass, it is only 2.4 km/s.

order.title: How the Moon moves outward
order.prompt: Put the steps of tidal friction in the order they happen, from the first step (bottom) to the last step (top).
order.why: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, so friction drags the tidal bulges slightly ahead of the Earth-Moon line. The gravity of those bulges then pulls the Moon forward, giving it orbital energy, so its orbit grows.

layers.name: Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits
Friction drags the tidal bulges ahead of the Earth-Moon line
The bulges' gravity pulls the Moon forward
The Moon moves to a larger orbit

order.title: Weigh the Sun
order.prompt: Put the steps for finding the Sun's mass from Earth's orbit in order, from the first step (bottom) to the last step (top).
order.why: Start with Newton's version of Kepler's third law. Earth is tiny, so the total mass is almost just the Sun's. Rearrange to get M = 4π² a³ / (G p²), put in the numbers, and calculate about 2 × 10³⁰ kg.

layers.name: Write Newton's version of Kepler's third law
Note that the Sun's mass is almost all the total
Put in p = 3.15 × 10⁷ s, a = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m and G

sort.title: Bound or unbound?
sort.prompt: Does each object or shape follow a bound orbit (goes around again and again) or an unbound orbit (passes once and never returns)?

items.text: An ellipse
A circle
A parabola
A hyperbola
Earth around the Sun
The Moon around Earth
A satellite circling Earth over and over
A comet that loops around the Sun once and never returns
A comet before it meets Jupiter, on an unbound path
The same comet after Jupiter took away enough energy
A spacecraft that reached escape velocity from Earth

sort.why: Ellipses (including circles) are the only bound shapes. Parabolas and hyperbolas are unbound. A comet that loses enough energy to Jupiter changes from unbound to bound, and a spacecraft that reaches escape velocity changes to an unbound path.

sort.title: What happens to the pull?
sort.prompt: Each change is made to two objects that attract each other with gravity. What happens to the force between them?

items.text: Both masses doubled, distance unchanged
Distance cut in half, masses unchanged
One mass quadrupled, distance unchanged
Distance doubled, masses unchanged
Both masses halved, distance unchanged
One mass cut to a quarter, distance unchanged
One mass quadrupled and distance quadrupled
Both masses doubled and distance doubled
Both masses tripled and distance tripled
One mass doubled and the other halved, distance unchanged
One mass quadrupled and distance doubled

sort.why: Turn each change into a factor: masses multiply on top, distance divides squared. For example one mass x4 and distance x4 gives 4 ÷ 16 = 1/4, while one mass x4 and distance x2 gives 4 ÷ 4 = 1.

sort.title: Spring or neap tide?
sort.prompt: Does each description belong to spring tides (the largest tides) or neap tides (the smaller tides)?

items.text: New Moon
Full Moon
First-quarter Moon
Third-quarter Moon
The Sun's and the Moon's tidal forces work together
The Sun's and the Moon's tidal forces work against each other
The largest tides of the month
The relatively small tides
Sun, Earth and Moon lie along one line
The water tends to spring up from Earth

sort.why: At new and full Moon the Sun and Moon stretch Earth along the same line, so their tidal forces add and the tides are largest. At the quarter Moons they work against each other and the tides are smaller.
